case.label: C
case.text: A CloudWatch alarm on the target group unhealthy host count that invokes a Lambda function calling SetInstanceHealth to mark each failing instance Unhealthy would also get the instances replaced automatically. It is a working workaround, but it needs custom code, an alarm and permissions, so it fails the LEAST operational overhead constraint against one setting in B. A and D are not possible: a target group cannot terminate instances, and there is no EBS health check type.

case.label: B
case.text: A launch lifecycle hook keeps the new instance in Pending:Wait until user data signals that the application answers. Health checks do not run during that state, so the replacement loop stops and later failures are still replaced. It works, but it needs a hook, a script change and the CLI call to complete the action, so it is more overhead than changing one grace period value. C is excluded because the stem says later failures must still be replaced. D is excluded because the cooldown governs scaling activities, not health check replacement.

answers.flag: The stem says the application cannot run as several copies, which rules out D, yet the stem also asks for handling daily peaks with minimal downtime, which B (a stop and start to resize) handles poorly; a careful candidate could defend D or B, so the constraints conflict.

case.label: D
case.text: D is the textbook scalable and highly available design (Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an ALB with target tracking), it handles daily peaks and long-term growth with the least downtime, and it is the only option that elastically follows load changes. The stem line that the application cannot run as several copies is the only thing against it, and a candidate could read that line as a constraint to be solved with sticky sessions or an externalised state. B needs a stop and start of the instance (downtime) at every resize and cannot follow daily peaks, so it conflicts with the minimal downtime requirement.
